body.text: Who would have thought that the Houthis, an obscure Iran-backed militia in Yemen, would snap the final threads of the fraying post-war order? On September 10, the Houthis marched down the Red Sea coast, exploiting a fracture between regional giants Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) frantically called US President Donald Trump for military support. He had been left stranded by the Emiratis and has been battered since July by Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy facilities, logistics, and tankers.

The US is a long-standing Saudi ally, and Trump maintains an unusual personal relationship with MBS. Trump’s first state visit in his first term was to Riyadh rather than—as is conventional—to Ottawa or Mexico City. Ostensibly, they would build a joint front against Iran. MBS heavily courted Trump, later investing $2 billion in Jared Kushner’s investment firm, cementing a financial bridge to a second term of the Trump administration. Yet, when the Saudis could not handle the Houthis, Trump declined to intervene militarily. Hours later, as the Houthis swept aside Saudi-backed forces and approached critical Red Sea choke points—the port city of Mocha and Perim Island across the narrow Strait of Bab el-Mandab—MBS called again. Trump declined again.

Almost simultaneously, Iran-backed insurgents in Iraq severely damaged Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which, with the Strait of Hormuz choked by Iran since March, was a critical oil conduit to the Red Sea. With that pipeline shut for weeks and the Houthis blocking the Red Sea’s southern exit, global oil supplies shrunk further.

These rapid-fire events shattered the teetering post-war equilibrium to create a new disorder. They marked the dramatic rise of a heavily armed, AI-literate non-state actor, the breakdown of cohesion among West Asian nations, and the fall of the American imperial project, which, though flawed, sustained global stability. The American imperium was already cracking because of the US’ own departures from international norms—an erosion Trump supercharged. The Houthis simply dismantled lingering illusions, pushing energy prices and bond yields further up.

The longer term disruption is frightening to contemplate. The simultaneous AI-powered levelling up of a non-state actor and the hollowing out of the world’s dominant power signal a terrifying proliferation of threats everywhere. There is no going back.
The Houthi phenomenon

The Houthis (who identify as Ansar Allah, or supporters of God) are no sandal-wearing, AK-47-toting stereotypes. They are modern guerrillas: a mobile, improvisational force fighting at multiple levels. While they still deploy rocket launchers bolted to truck beds, they also possess an astonishing array of advanced weaponry, as catalogued by The Hague Institute for Geopolitics.

Above all, they represent the radical levelling unleashed by AI, demonstrating how little human expertise is required to develop advanced weapons. Any agile group can tap into this “third force”, breaching tech majors’ improvised firewalls to match the strategic leverage once monopolised by the great powers. In a fascinating disclosure, the AI firm Anthropic reported that a north Yemen–based “cell of threat actors” (though unnamed, almost certainly the Houthis) used its signature Claude Code to design sophisticated firepower. This included a guided rocket with final-phase homing, a multi-stage ballistic missile with an intended 2,000 kilometre range, and a multivariant missile featuring a hypersonic glide vehicle.
“MBS spent years buying American weaponry and cultivating the Trump family only to discover that the US’ protection against the Houthis was an illusion.”

Claude Code is especially powerful for non-programmers. It requires only high-level instructions on goals and constraints; the AI then determines the most efficient coding and writes procedures to test its integrity. The Houthi designers used Claude with chilling intelligence. They specified easy-to-procure components available through legal or black market channels, fragmented their sessions to evade Anthropic’s safety guard rails, and went offline to continue simulated testing once they suspected detection.
The West Asia Fracture

While the Houthis had long menaced shipping lanes, the collapse of the Saudi-UAE axis removed the primary military barrier to their coastal advance. Saudi Arabia remains the region’s heavyweight, but a UAE intent on modernising its economy fiercely resisted being perceived as a Saudi vassal. In Yemen, the two powers had maintained an uneasy peace via distinct proxy zones. The Saudis backed the central government, while the UAE supported the Southern Transitional Council, which sought an independent southern state. Although ideologically at odds, these factions wereheld together solely by their shared opposition to the Houthis.

This fragile arrangement shattered in late 2025 when Saudi air strikes targeted military equipment originating from a UAE port, prompting the UAE to withdraw its remaining logistics from southern Yemen. This rupture dissolved the anti-Houthi coalition. The Hindu highlighted the consequences of a fractured Yemen on the Persian Gulf’s geopolitical fault line, alongside subsequent diplomatic signals of a rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and the UAE—a truce that never materialised.

Now, as the sole external patron of a fractured Yemeni government, Saudi Arabia was left with deeply divided, poorly integrated ground forces, many of which were easily bought off by Houthi cash. Rearmed during the preceding lull, the Houthis launched a mid-July offensive that culminated in their swift September sweep of the Yemeni west coast, exposing the inability of Saudi-backed forces to defend the Red Sea choke points.

MBS spent years buying hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of American weaponry and cultivating the Trump family for exactly this scenario. Yet, the inexperienced Saudi military discovered that the US’ necessary additional protection against the highly motivated Houthis was an illusion. With the US forces plagued by resource depletion from a six-month confrontation with Iran, Trump had nothing but basic intelligence and logistics to offer a panicky MBS.

The US military could, in principle, have blown up Perim Island, but that risked stirring a geopolitical hornets’ nest a badly stretched US fleet could not contain. Trump and everyone else are stymied by their recent experience of the Iranian calculus that dictates reactive assaults on US-affiliated targets regardless of immediate losses.

The Saudis also have a mutual defence pact with Türkiye and Pakistan, signed barely a month earlier, on August 7. As Houthi attacks escalated on Riyadh and Yanbu (where the Saudis store vast amounts of oil), the Turks offered words of solidarity but held back military support. Pakistan reiterated “unconditional” commitment to Saudi Arabia but, nursing a “crippled” economy, could not afford engagement in “a never-ending” crisis. Now the Saudis are completely exposed and West Asia is adrift.

In the 1880s, German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck observed: “One day the great European War will come out of some damned foolish thing in the Balkans.” The Houthis are no fools, but the warning is clear.
Decline of the US imperium

The US had maintained the aura of the postwar order’s all-powerful armed force, capable of being a protective presence across critical geopolitical zones. That military aura gave it a decisive say in global trade and finance. The dollar, by virtue of network externalities—where others use it because everyone else does—made the US a financial juggernaut. That, in essence, was the US imperium.
“The Houthis are no sandal-wearing, AK-47-toting stereotypes. They are modern guerrillas: a mobile, improvisational force fighting at multiple levels.”

But this dominance relied as much on myth as on reality. Despite a conventional triumph in the 1991 Gulf War blitzkrieg, the US faced repeated humiliations: from Vietnam to the grinding, decades-long occupations of Afghanistan and Iraq. Time and again, much weaker armies have waged prolonged guerrilla warfare to defend their very existence. In Trump’s Iran war, the US fell into a modern variation of this trap. Iran and its proxies paired traditional guerrilla evasion with cheap precision weaponry. Throughout these military adventures, the US killed large numbers of civilians with no evident accountability. A UN panel has accused the US of war crimes in the killing of Iranian schoolchildren.

Despite vast military inferiority, Iran inflicted substantial damage on regional US bases, the full extent of which American authorities are only slowly revealing. One service member exclaimed: “We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.” More US soldiers have died in Iran than what was until recently reported. Meanwhile, to pursue its Iran adventure, the US has pulled substantial troops and firepower from the Indo-Pacific theatre, where it was the presumed guardian of peace. Many Taiwanese now believe that America will not defend them—a deal with China seems inevitable.

Today, the US faces a debilitating depletion of munitions, especially advanced missile interceptors. Continuous deployments and deferred maintenance of carrier fleets during the blockade of Iran have created severe vulnerabilities, including a shortage of strike-fighter pilots. “More and more,” writes the military historian Phillips O’Brien, “the American emperor is exposed as having ‘no clothes’.” The US military has failed, O’Brien says, because of “material failure in preparing US forces”, worsened by “dishonesty” in acknowledging losses and by endemic “corruption”.

In trade, the US flouted the rules it helped establish and benefited from. Faced with Japanese competition in the 1980s, the US turned against its own free market rhetoric and coerced Japan into voluntary export restraints. China’s subsequent rise created a fierce bipartisan consensus that it was “cheating”, justifying the barring of Chinese imports (I saw China’s BYD electric car for the first time on a recent visit to Ireland) and restricting access to foundational US technology. The Joe Biden administration subscribed to this protectionist view as aggressively as Trump does. Trump simply added bizarre, volatile tariffs to the mix.
“China, possibly the only winner in this churn, is inching ahead to replace US hegemony.”

Similarly, the US weaponised dollar dominance via financial sanctions, which went on steroids after 9/11. Justified by the battle against terrorism, the USA PATRIOT Act dismantled the traditional insulation of international banking from foreign policy. Trump is distinct not in this choke-point control over international financial flows but in his whimsical deployment of it.

Unique to Trump is rampant market price manipulation by political insiders. Large financial bets placed just before he announced an imminent Iran “deal” have set a dangerous precedent. While these announcements are losing credibility, the norm is broken, and others will copy the tactic.
The reckoning

This was never merely an energy shock; it was a broader blow to the global industrial system. The Gulf states are “industrial giants” whose chemical outputs “sustain industries and food systems across continents”. The crisis has since evolved into a geopolitical transformation, with a minor non-state actor emerging as a lethal arbiter in global affairs.

China, possibly the only winner in this churn, is inching ahead to replace US hegemony. But for India, as for most developing economies, the West Asia upheaval has sent energy, especially natural gas, prices shooting up. Compounded by rising shipping and insurance costs and by a severely constrained supply of petrochemical derivatives, fertilizers, and intermediate industrial products critical to manufacturing, global price pressures will bubble for years. Interest rates will therefore remain elevated, weakening the global economy. This is a severe blow to India’s high-cost, uncompetitive economy, straining corporate balance sheets and the government’s fiscal position.

The unique post-war order—forged by memories of the Great Depression and the Second World War—gave special accommodation to developing nations, granting them latitude to use tariffs and barriers to protect domestic production. As those memories have faded, global competition has turned harsher with a dominating zero-sum mentality. The diminishing space for development could vanish entirely.

Ultimately, the unpredictable reordering of the world poses the deepest threat. Will the UAE—with whom India has rapidly bound its economic future and which serves as a sanctuary for the Indian elite—survive under Iran’s cold gaze? Will India’s signature stance of “multi-alignment” remain viable? Can it maintain ties with Israel and the UAE while balancing a necessary relationship with Iran? Could it continue to play off rival weak-kneed superpowers?

In the summer, I warned that a dark winter loomed. Such realism is often dismissed as unwarranted pessimism by observers who mistake their nostalgia for lost certainties as optimism. It is a continuing liberal conceit that once Trump exits, the world will seamlessly return to predictable, even benign, post-war arrangements. History, however, is a cruel master. The post-war order lost its material, political, and—most importantly—reputational foundations because the US exploited and undermined its own system for too long; Trump merely supercharged that erosion. Trump will go, but there is no liberal nirvana to go back to. That the obscure Houthis could expose this denouement so decisively proves how fragile the old order was, and serves as an ominous warning of the coming disorder.
Ashoka Mody retired from Princeton University. He previously worked for the World Bank and the IMF. He is the author of India is Broken: A People Betrayed, Independence to Today (2023).
